A printed bookplate for Emmanuel College, Cambridge. It features a heraldic shield with a lion rampant (a lion standing on its hind legs), facing left, holding a laurel wreath in its paws. Above the lion is a banner with the word **EMMANUEL** <note>original: "ΕΜΜΑΝΟΥΗΛ", the Greek transcription of the Hebrew name meaning "God with us," which is the namesake of the college</note>. At the bottom corners of the shield are the signatures "Stephens, engraver" <note>original: "Stephens sculp.", an abbreviation of the Latin "sculpsit," meaning "he carved or engraved this"</note> and "Cambridge" <note>original: "Cantab.", an abbreviation for "Cantabrigia," the Latin name for Cambridge</note>.

<meta>This page begins a 14th-century astrological treatise by the English scholar John Ashenden. He is writing during the height of the Black Death (1348-1349), attempting to explain the pandemic through the movements of the planets, specifically the "conjunctions" (alignments) of Saturn, Mars, and Jupiter.</meta>

## Here begins the treatise of John Ashenden, formerly a fellow of Merton Hall in Oxford, on the signifi-
## cance of the conjunction of Saturn and Mars in Cancer, which will occur in this year of Christ 1348, on the eighth day
## of June; and on the significance of this great conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter, which will occur in the year of our Lord 1349, on the 30th day
## of October at the 4th hour and 22nd minute.

As Ptolemy says in the *Centiloquium* <note>original: "centilogio"; a famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to the ancient astronomer Claudius Ptolemy</note>, proposition 48: many things happen in the world due to the movement of the fixed stars and the wandering stars <note>original: "errantium"; the planets</note>. These movements are the primary cause of things that have happened in this world or are yet to come. Masha'allah <note>original: "messahalla"; an influential 8th-century Persian Jewish astronomer and astrologer</note> agrees with him in his letter on conjunctions, saying that every planet signifies effects from a greater cause in this manner. Specifically, in his first prologue, he puts forward this opinion regarding the conjunction that is forbidden by the ancients. And according to his opinion, and again by the counsel on the 20-year cycles and the 120-year cycles of the planets... as is clear through Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraham avenezram"; a 12th-century Spanish scholar</note> in his book *On the Years of the World*, where he says, as Masha'allah states, that great matters and palaces <note>The text reads "palate," which may be a transcription error for "palam" (openly/publicly) or "palatia" (palaces)</note> come to pass from the conjunctions of the planets, and this happens according to the fortune and the slowness of their motion. 

According to the same opinion of Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Albumazar"; a 9th-century Persian astrologer whose work was the standard for medieval Europe</note> in the first and second parts of his book *On the Great Conjunctions*. And since this occurs in the year of our Lord 1348, in the month of June, on the eve and the 22nd day of that same month, at 22 hours and 38 minutes before noon <note>Medieval astronomers often calculated the day starting from noon</note>, the meeting of Saturn and Mars in the sign of Cancer... and according to the end of the world <note>original: "secundum finem... mundi"; likely referring to the current age or world-cycle</note> as their closest associate says. And in the sign of the world in the year of our Lord 1349, in the month of October, on the eve and the 29th day of the same month, at 18 hours and 22 minutes before noon, there will be a conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter in the sign of Scorpio. This belongs to the ninth triplicity <term>Triplicity|A group of three zodiac signs associated with one of the four elements (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water). Scorpio is a Water sign.</term> which will signify very many mutations <note>change or transformations</note> in the world and in the waters around India and Ethiopia, according to the astronomers who speak on this matter. 

And therefore, since they differ regarding the meanings of these two conjunctions—sometimes in one way and sometimes in another—if any others had wished to write on this matter, many great nobles could have shown themselves graciously through other treatises. But they have refused to show their knowledge and the depth of this book because of the labor of others. They were also burdened by their own resources, and they disparaged themselves and others most wickedly. For it did not profit them to show the whole truth of these accidents <note>historical events or occurrences</note>, but they grieve miserably and defame others. 

I, however, wish to extract a few points concerning the manner and significations of these two conjunctions from the books of the astronomers, and to record them in their volumes. I protest that I wish to show the sayings of the astrologers for those to whom the truth is not clear. I have set down nothing of my own invention <note>original: "de capite proprio"; literally "from my own head"</note>; nothing could or should be emitted except what is extended from the books of the astrologers. 

There follows the distinction of the conjunction of Saturn and Mars in Cancer, which will be in the year of our Lord 1348, in the month of June, on the eve of the 22nd day, at 22 hours and 38 minutes.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of planetary conjunctions, moving from general principles of duration and efficacy to specific authorities like Albumasar and Masha'allah. It concludes by applying these theories to a significant historical event: the Great Conjunction of September 30, 1364.</meta>

According to the consensus of astronomers and astrologers, the greater the power of a **conjunction** <note>original: "conjunctione"; the alignment of two or more planets in the same sign of the zodiac</note>, the more delayed its effect will be; yet, by that same measure, the effect will endure much longer. Conversely, the more a conjunction is hindered or weakened, the sooner its effects will manifest, but they will persist through all times with less stability. This is in accordance with **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a Persian astrologer whose *Great Conjunctions* was a standard textbook in medieval Europe</note>, who discusses the "whole" and the "part" and what is owed to the greater of the two. In that conjunction, the power of the motion which occurs will determine the effects that are generated; they will begin within the duration of that time.

These effects are made manifest in the signs of many storms, winds, thunders, lightnings, and other phenomena which reveal the efficacy of the work. Indeed, the fate of these things will occur within their conjunction. And not only in their conjunction, but through the motion, application, and deeds found in the signs, as well as the lordship of the motion.

We must also consider the timing through the **Moon** ☾, and the "aspect" <note>the angular distance between planets, believed to transmit their influence</note> that assists in this. If other planets assist in this, it is well; but other greater impressions—such as a conjunction, a "beneficence," and the like—may produce effects that are similarly delayed. It is said that for some, the effect appears after 40 days, for others after 3 months from the time of the event, and for others even later if the planets were of greater power. These effects, in their own time, possess a more lordly efficacy than those which appear immediately after the conjunction.

This arises from the **fortitude** and **debility** <note>technical terms for the strength or weakness of a planet based on its position in the zodiac</note> of both planets. If the "lords" <note>planets that rule the specific signs where the event occurs</note> are strong, they will exercise their power in their own signs. If they are weak, the duration of the effect will be lessened, as shown in the summary of Albumasar's second book on Great Conjunctions. If, for instance, they are in the "angles" <note>the four most powerful houses of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note>, the duration and efficacy are extended.

Furthermore, consider the nature of the signs as described by Albumasar:
- When the great planets are in **movable signs** <note>original: "signis mobilibus"; also called Cardinal signs (Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn), associated with change and initiation</note>, they signify a local change or movement.
- When they are in **fixed signs** <note>original: "signis fixis"; (Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius), associated with stability and persistence</note>, they signify firmness and permanence.
- When they are in **corporeal signs** <note>original: "signis corporeis"; also called Mutable or common signs (Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces)</note>, they signify a "mediocrity" or a middle ground between change and stability.

The authority **Messehalla** <note>original: "Messehalla"; Masha'allah ibn Athari (c. 740–815 AD), a Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer</note> agrees in his own summary of conjunctions. He states that if a conjunction occurs in fixed signs, it signifies the stability of an evil and its eventual corruption. If in movable signs, it signifies a lack of stability in that evil. Similarly, in corporeal signs, it signifies a moderate state in both evil and good.

This is not only found in the stars or in their own movements, but in the "houses." Even if a planet is not in a fixed sign but in a movable one, its greater strength or debility must be weighed.

According to the summary of Albumasar's second book, regarding the lords... and the moderate efficacy of a great action in the lives of men. This depends on the quantity of the lords and the arc of the presiding planets in that conjunction, specifically regarding the change of life and peace.

This conjunction of lords is significant; the **Moon** ☾ is especially the measurer. By following the calculations of Albumasar regarding the arcs and the time of the Moon, which is 39, and the remaining 28, it is clear that the effect in these conjunctions lasts for 20 years.

But in truth, let us look toward the year of our Lord **1364**, on the 30th day of September <note>This refers to the Great Conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter in the sign of Scorpio, a major event for medieval political prophecy</note>. This was a very great sign of transitions, as is evident. The efficacy of this event is more powerful in its fate and will endure until the next conjunction. It has been 8 years since that event <note>indicating the manuscript was likely being written or revised around 1372</note>. When the stars are "bound" together in their own power, this bond remains firm throughout the years, unless another application of the stars creates a contrary influence. Therefore, the effect of this conjunction is 20 years and more, remaining firm through the bonds of the lords.

### Conclusion of Josua de Fubens

<margin>+</margin> Since the science of astrology <note>original: "scia astrologia"</note> is, among others, the way toward the perfection of my intellect regarding the highest prediction of future things—since in these times, as it has always been, the superior power works through prophets and subsequently through presence and genius—God knows that if the Lord of the time is in the present prediction, which lies in these astral paths because of the spirit entering at that time, it is enough to say: in that which will be brought forth and directed. For there are things to come through this art by which a man can attain to the human and divine matters of the gods. That which is to come through the superior stars is clear. And therefore I, Joshua de Fubens of Pavia, formerly physician of blessed memory to the most illustrious prince Lord John, Duke of Burgundy <note>referring to John the Fearless, 1371–1419</note>, humbly implore my Creator. That He may therefore direct me as much as I am able to describe the universal events of the present year and of the other stars, to make a judgment from this point until the end of the year 1521. This regards August, on the eleventh day, at the month's fourteenth hour, 29 minutes—which is for the midday. On which day and hour, the Lord of the year and the ruler, the Sun, holds its course toward the financial state <note>original: "situ financie"</note>, where in this judgment he places many evils and adversities, which sign is openly to come. Concerning these hours, one ought not to tremble, because through his free will <note>original: "liberum arbitrium"</note> and wisdom, these evil adversities can be avoided. For as the wise man says, he shall possess all things, and thus to this end are the judgments of the stars, so that he might know these approaching things according to the Lord. Therefore, since there is an eclipse which, on account of the present Lord of the markets and by merit of the penury we suffer, shows his power in the year 1521, which regards the month of August on the 20th day, 22nd minute, and clearly at the 4th hour, 15th minute. [further details] in the 3rd book below. Whence he was the Lord, who in another place and power by merit in which he is present, namely, it is discovered in this second eclipse of the moon which will occur on the 11th of February, after the setting of the sun at the 8th hour after midday, at the financial state, and it will have its true effect through my presence in the holy [year] as predicted by me, etc. The eclipse will be on the 13th day of August before midday, at the 12th hour of the kingdom... as it will be in the transit toward my position... it will give much that the eclipse of the moon prepares in that penury through my Lord; they will be adverse. <meta>This page continues the commentary by John of Saxony on the "Introduction to the Art of Judgment" by Alchabitius (al-Qabisi). -># John of Saxony on Alchabitius, page 24<-

**That the wise man shall rule the stars:** <note>original: "Sapiens dominabitur astris". This was a cornerstone of medieval astrological ethics, suggesting that while stars influence the physical world, human reason remains free.</note> this is a proposition found in the more learned *Almagest*. <note>The *Almagest* is Ptolemy's foundational work on astronomy, though this specific quote is often associated with the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 aphorisms attributed to him.</note> And it is declared by that saying that the stars produce effects coming out of those very stars because of a lack of hindrance. But a **wise man** can do this <insert>hinder them</insert> because he is greater, for he who rules does what he does by the authority of the philosophers. For Hippocrates <note>original: "ypo(cras)". The text refers to a pseudo-Hippocratic work on astrology.</note> in the *Centiloquium* says that the utility of the stars prohibits much evil, because the stars are foreseen. And therefore, because nature provides for everything, when an evil is found to be coming, one is able to endure it when it arrives. And because matter is accustomed, just as in its own [nature?], so the wise man will help [mitigate] the stars... <unclear>d</unclear>... <unclear>s</unclear>

The wise man prevents or assists the work of the stars. Although it is said that no one can always hinder the celestial efficacy, it is a misuse <note>of the term</note> if we say we can dispose ourselves to receive the action and celestial influence. Just as we see that the heat of the sun dissolves ice but hardens clay. <note>A common medieval metaphor: the same celestial cause (the sun) has different effects based on the material it hits.</note> And Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> speaks of these things from the seventh commentary regarding the specific properties of the works of the stars. He says that if a scholar knows that a hot and dry change is coming in the nature of the atmosphere, he can, by reason, change [his situation] to the opposite before the arrival of that influence.

And yet it is a great hindrance to declare those things which are removable. Just as it is said that a man can be moved away from a fire; so the science [of astrology] makes one a ruler. The Masters are the "educators" and are seen among those wise men of whom many words are spoken. <meta>This page continues the discussion from page 24 regarding the philosophical and ethical requirements of the astrologer. Having established that a "wise man rules the stars," John of Saxony now elaborates on the specific qualities—such as stability, humility, and poverty—that allow a practitioner to achieve such wisdom, drawing heavily on Ptolemy’s *Centiloquium* and the commentaries of Haly.</meta>

<margin>
To them belongs: 1. stability of intention / 2. humility of discipline / 3. renunciation of earthly possession / for so it is said by **Ptolemy** in the 2nd [aphorism], when he says the "wise man" [rules the stars], and 3rd when it is said [the soul] will inhabit the stars. <note>original: "eis ē stabilitas intenciōis / 2. humilitas disciplīe / 3. abdicatio terrēe possessiōis". These are the classic three requirements for an astrologer according to the pseudo-Ptolemaic *Centiloquium*.</note>
</margin>

What is said regarding the first question by **Ptolemy** <note>original: "Ptholōms"</note> in the first aphorism of the *Centiloquium* <note>original: "p̄m̄o p̄noē octīdēm". The *Centiloquium* is a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms.</note> is that a certain error exists in time... which **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel or Haly ibn Ridwan, famous Arabic commentators on Ptolemy.</note> in his commentary explains, saying that those desires which are to be pre-defined ought to yield to the stars at all times. And he grasps the movement of the stars through works which are not in things according to the movement of their causes. And it appears to the free will concerning the signs that the movements of the epicycles <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in Ptolemaic astronomy to explain planetary paths.</note> are made. And let there be joined to this as much as is proven in its own time with great labor and the assiduous movement of the stars; it cannot be brought forth by an astronomer concerning the remission [of influence]. For when the limited time goes out toward the lower [world], the free will cannot wander from the works which, as astrologers [say], are according to the finality of the intention. Thus, it is achieved by being released from the star or repelled.

As for the second [question], which is said concerning **Ptolemy**, <insert>A</insert> in the arrangement of the titles: no one would be able to give divine judgments through the stars unless he knows all the ways in which the applications of their natures are well-known. He wishes, therefore, that for that person there must be a disposition toward this science which is called the "office of the soul." <note>original: "officie m̄ sa." referring to the *officium animae*.</note> He always seems to have one special science above all others. He mentions "good theology" and "natural philosophy," without which one will not be able to grasp anything of astronomy. [This is for] the most religious and pious ones, who by nature are disposed to or repelled from astronomy. Concerning these things, **Albumasar** <note>original: "albū ala-", referring to Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a leading Persian astrologer.</note> makes [mention], according to what is seen immediately in **Ptolemy** regarding the 3rd [point].

Regarding the indicators which are held in the commentary of the highest promise: it is necessary not to be solicitous concerning mundane affairs or the riches of the world for the purpose of knowing the future. <insert>which</insert>... so that we might be able to prognosticating the ends [of things]. Just as hermits and those who labor in philosophy <note>original: "heremitās & p̄ll’o".</note> [do], who operate in the ends of things. Should one not hold [to this] for the sake of bodily senses? Concerning the words of God, it is said through the astrologer that they ought not be rich. **Ptolemy** <note>original: "p̄th̄ō"</note> says it is not necessary for a philosopher to be rich in land or sea, but it suffices that he has a small amount, being insufficient in himself; otherwise, those having the riches of this world are repelled from <term>astrology</term> <note>original: "ast̄lōgia". The text argues that worldly greed clouds the clarity of mind needed for accurate prediction.</note>. As it is added, <term>Empedocles</term> <note>Empedocles (c. 494–434 BC), a Greek philosopher who, according to legend, cast his wealth into the sea to better pursue wisdom.</note> threw [his gold] into the sea.

<insert>B</insert> / In this, certain things do not please me much, since in the midst of these conditions, **Albumasar** <note>original: "albū"</note> brings us a great deduction of errors to be observed. Which changes when [applied] to the work. I say that perhaps water does not suffice for wisdom... they have assigned these in an abundance of things... it is possible to repel error from oneself because of the brevity of the speech... of all things which are known through them.

In the second place, regarding the conditions, not a few are reported. Because the time of man is brief, perhaps many of those things which could be apprehended are not sufficient. For then there are the sciences of the masters of treatises, which are the nature or the property of things in the depths... as to the 2nd [point]: that [the astrologer] should not be wealthy, it should not be wondered at... and few are found who are perfected in the medicine of wisdom. This is compared to the astrologer who operates... in astrology more than in any other science. And if they fail in the cause of errors, it is more tolerable since it harms less than what is seen in other sciences. And what is said of that same medicine in the beginning: in many diseases, it is given [as a sign] that they happen in the end because of the quantity of the disease, with lightness and with speed of facility. It is with slowness [that one moves] toward health or death.

But those small medical errors do not hinder them from the appearance of mastery, according to his disposition and generation... it is not generated by an incomprehension or doubt of men toward those to whom it seems, from the mode of their errors in the end, that the utility and perfection [is great] because of their eminence and the acquisition of their medicines. So it is in the proportions of natures: they do not diminish their mastery, nor do they diminish a man's sense of the sea if there is a small error of the sailors <note>original: "nautaꝝ". A common medieval analogy: a pilot may make a small mistake, but he is still a master of the ship.</note>. Since the science of things is from the mouth of the authors, they can always escape before the crown of old age is hindered... so that a man does not lose his mastery. And in this, the impediment of errors is more for the reason of the astrologers than for the physicians when they err in their own infirmity, either in reason or in medicines. Perhaps also in the three aforesaid [conditions]... when sailors err, perhaps with this cause... And if astrologers err, the master of astrology [Ptolemy] says it is the ignorance of the inferior parts [of the art]... not in the seeking of the cause of horrible things before they happen... and perhaps those things...

<meta>This page continues the defense of astrology, moving from the physical "complexions" of bodies discussed on page 25 to the philosophical and theological justification of the science. It establishes astrology as the study of time and providence, distinguishing human intelligence from animal instinct by the ability to foresee the future through celestial motions.</meta>

In excellence, and to know through the dignity of man <note>The "dignity of man" refers to the medieval philosophical concept that humans are superior to animals because they possess reason and the ability to understand their place in time.</note> over other animals, is nothing if not through the knowledge of things which have been and which <margin>10</margin> are to come. And from these things it is reported, as it is said, that through the dignity of things in time and in future ages, it looks out when it arises and exists; in its uncertainty it has its own mastery. And concerning the order of the motion of the celestial bodies, that which is sought to be known is said to be through the knowledge of the species, although a multitude of errors has been said to exist among humans who follow this science. Concerning these people, who detract from the sense of the world and the open world, that power is driven away, and it raises the masters from here to behold it. And they say that it is a hollow science because of another reason: that this is not experienced in the grade of the masters of this science. For the proper characteristics of those who follow it are that they are humble in spirit, chaste, and abundant in resources. And that which responds is properly of the men who are masters, led into graces and seductions, and they lead back the weak with many sayings—that which operates through geometry and through the property of astronomy, just as [they are] not men and sciences which are for profit; and yet it is said that this science is terminated from water even unto water, that it might lead the steps and compare the [balances] of the chaste and of his Almighty.

But this science of sciences is from those sayings, for it is said that this science is true faith, and so I say. It responds to reading <margin>11</margin> among the books of the ancient sages who wrote about this science; it permits the world—not the doctors of this science—because another thing is the first foundation of faith. And these are **Haly Abenragel** <note>original: "Haly abenragel," referring to the 11th-century Arab astrologer Albohazen Haly filius Abenragel, whose "Book of the Judgments of the Stars" was a standard text.</note> in the first part of his book, in the chapter on proper nature: that at the time when God created the world, he placed Jupiter in the Ascendant <note>This refers to the "Thema Mundi," the mythical horoscope of the world's creation.</note> and elsewhere. In the title of his guide, just as we say first, that the motion of the others, the lords, is regulated by the virtue of the First Cause <note>The "First Cause" is a philosophical term for God as the ultimate source of all motion in the universe.</note> over the chapters that are across the earth in the celestial bodies, and the appetites and motions which come to humans; because this power is primary, it was immutable and incorruptible. And they do not exalt every quality in them, just as it is read in the disposition. I shall expedite myself briefly and set down the divisions which he places elsewhere in his Great Introductory. There are two species of astronomy: one is practical and the science of the stars and times in things; and the other is the judgment of the stars <note>term: "indiciaastrorum" (judicial astrology). This refers to the practice of making predictions based on planetary positions.</note>. **Ptolemy** <note>The 2nd-century Alexandrian polymath whose works formed the basis of medieval astronomy.</note> places this division in the first distinction of his science; he has it in the commentary in the same place in the first part, and all of it perfectly and completely as to the principles of the science. For Ptolemy in the *Almagest* <note>The definitive medieval textbook on astronomy.</note> placed himself with the proximate and remote sciences concerning motions and the complexes of the science and the **ephemerides** <note>term: "ephemerides." These are mathematical tables used to calculate the daily positions of planets.</note> which are called tabular. These ephemerides are inspected so that they may be applied to observations; the motions are estimated just as Ptolemy correctly administered and composed them elsewhere, so that these many things [are] principally continuous and returning as if they were special. A solid science of wisdom and a science in all species of gods, or of the judgments of the stars, as there are principal parts which are by the method of **interrogations** and of **nativities**, of the **revolutions** of years, and of the **elections** of hours. <note>These are the four traditional branches of astrology: Interrogations (answering specific questions), Nativities (birth charts), Revolutions (annual world forecasts), and Elections (choosing the best time for an event).</note> And **Haly Abenragel** did this in the introduction of the years of the world in the time of the profit of the years of nativities, concerning things and perils. **Haly Abenragel** made one complete book through eight distinctions, in all two parts: namely, concerning interrogations and the elections of hours, which Haly—who contains it—excuses him by saying that he thought these two parts were from the books where Ptolemy is in the same place and notes them. And as for the other parts of judgments—namely, concerning wars and the <margin>impacts</margin> of masters in the individual abundances and concerning those <insert>**Almansor**</insert> <note>original: "Almansor," likely referring to Yahya ibn Abi Mansur, a 9th-century astronomer at the court of al-Ma'mun.</note>—it is in the time that the first of the ancients among many masters was introduced, because those parts were difficult to interpret. Concerning those things, they first made a trial in the books of the skilled ones, which first arrived and exposed them just as the masters of the Indians are [well-received], and as from other books of the guide’s book elsewhere, and the masters approved in many ways. I have left that to others concerning things for this order, to your teaching proposed to the Lord, it is prepared for this: that is, in the preface of this book there are four things which are necessary for a book. First is the utility; second, what is the title of this book; third, in what part it is placed; fourth, what it teaches—sixteenth, what they say [like] the eagle concerning the division of the books. The intention of the book is likewise to make the science prompt, because in reality and with this nature and times, one learns the judgments of the stars. And the utility—which is evident through all things—is that it is a good science for the teaching of humans in the time of the pressed books and the rest, as if, if well understood, it could [encompass] the eight books of the world.

One should not understand this by itself. The book itself states its own division into two parts: 
1. The first part concerns physics and practiced experiments; he speaks in the first night to God. 
2. The second, called the executive part, is in four parts. 

What the author sees in his own [work], which he calls the four, is clear through the 26th [chapter] of the physics... the whole is stated in the second part because in the first part he invokes divine help—that is, through the application he opens his [intentions]. ### **On the Division**
**In this he teaches** <note>original: "In hoc docet"</note>—in this division he first shows and asks for a prayer from God for his status so that he may complete his work. He also asks for the lasting honor of the King's sword for his protection and for the application of himself.

He says that he saw many ancients had made introductory books to the science of the stars, but from them, one could not clearly grasp the intention, because they handed down what they had seen too prolixly <note>meaning "at too great a length"</note> and because they were obscure. Their books are obscured by their own [style], and yet that [science] is born to be helpful. He intends not to bypass their discipline. Therefore, he sees such things and from them he collected this book, and from those ancients, he put forth those things which were born to be helpful. 

**In this he teaches:** Here he excuses himself regarding the terminology, so that one might not [stumble] on these words. In this part, two doubts may be moved. The first is about the number of signs; the second is about their order.

According to Albur, it is said that through this it is evident, etc.

# On the Zones

At this point, a question may be raised: is the region under the equator habitable? If so, why is it said that people do not live there? <gloss>m</gloss> <insert>your only [concern]</insert> The sun does not perpetually wear down that part, and it wears it down only slightly since it [the sun] has been above it. There are five zones in the heavens: one is the torrid zone, which is always under the equator and extends from its own parts to the tropics <note>original: "epicos"; likely a transcription error for "tropicos"</note>; others are under the poles and are said to be uninhabitable in the middle because of that uninhabitable rising; the torrid zone is uninhabitable because of excessive heat, and the two extreme zones under the poles are uninhabitable because of excessive cold. The other two zones are temperate because of their mildness.

I believe, however, that it should be admitted that the region under the equator is habitable—and indeed, it is the best place for habitation. I offer this reason which moves me: where there is the best habitation, there is also the greatest moderation of climate <note>original: "temp[er]ies"; referring to the balance of heat and cold</note>. But under the equator, there is the greatest moderation; therefore, it is the best. I declare this further: at the equator, the days are never unequal <note>original: "n[un]q[uam] sep[ar]at[e] equales"; meaning they are always equal</note>, and the coldness of the air at night cools the earth just as the sun heats it by day. Because the declination varies more in its change of declination in a single day... perhaps in one part it is said that if the sun passes directly over their heads, it does not recede toward the poles... and then they call it a day, because the sun remains at the same height above them. It is well governed if there is motion in the present, though the altitude may lack. Because only in this way does the sun move so much that it recedes from the day... where there is more heating, it is necessary for the rays to be tempered by water. For if we see in the present the burning of the East, it moves as much as it does not recede... and the other which opposes it by perpetual cold and chilliness... so there should be a greater heat. In truth, as I say—saving their grace <note>original: "salva g[rat]ia eorum"; a polite way of disagreeing with established authorities</note>—the same cause of cold will not be so cold in the middle parts of the earth as it would be in the [extreme] parts of the world. <gloss>v</gloss> and <gloss>v</gloss> can be in this [zone] then. <margin>Concerning the four seasons</margin>
### The Four Seasons and the Ages of Man

The first part, from Aries to the end of <note>The text says Sagittarius here, but immediately corrects the divisions in the following lines to follow the standard three-month seasons.</note> is the hot half because it creates summer for us, and the other half is cold because it creates winter for us. And note those four parts of these twelve signs according to the four seasons of the year by reason of their properties: summer <note>Likely meaning Spring in this context of the first quadrant</note> is from the first of Aries to the end of Gemini; it is hot and moist, just as is the first age of **puberty**, because beginnings are both hot and moist. Following this is the second age of puberty or **adolescence** leading into youth. The next part is from the first of Cancer to the first of Libra; it is hot and dry, just as summer is, and its property is **choleric**. From the first of Libra to the first of Capricorn, it is cold and dry, just as autumn is; this is the third age, which is the first stage of **decline**, and its property is **melancholic**. Finally, from the first of Capricorn to the end of Pisces, it is cold and moist, just as winter is; this is the **decrepit** age, and its property is **phlegm**. 

<margin>How a planet is in a sign</margin>
It is said that a planet has an order in the signs. Regarding how a planet is received in a sign, it is divided into three parts; it never has a triplicity <term>Triplicity: A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</term> receiving the signs in the way the author sets down here. It is noted that a planet takes its grace or beauty from a cause; it is said to take it from the heat as they are in the signs, as the planet wishes to manifest in its parts. Hence, planets in the signs are authorities regarding the diminution of anything, just as it is with signs that have that same disposition. Here, he wishes to speak of the **dignities** <term>Dignities: A system of "essential" strengths that make a planet more powerful or favorable depending on its location in the zodiac.</term>: first of **Exaltations**, second of **Houses**. 

### The Five Essential Dignities

A planet in its exaltation [is powerful], and thus there are twelve signs. The first two parts make the planets' dignities within the signs. In the second part, he determines the fortunate aspects they have in those dignities. By the authority of God, it is first said that there are many parts. There are **5 dignities** by which he first determines the power of the planets: 
1. The first is called **House** (*Domus*).
2. The second is called **Exaltation** (*Exaltatio*).
3. The third is called **Triplicity** (*Triplicitas*).
4. The fourth is called **Terms** (*Termini*).
5. The fifth is called **Face** (*Facies*). 

Secondly, where there is Exaltation; thirdly, in Triplicity and dignities, and so on, as they are in each sign. Where a "Face" is concerned, it is divided into parts. The first shows the properties of all the planets, while the second part shows each of them individually and appropriately. Each also has two houses, because one is more principal, and that is called the one in which the planet **rejoices**; he shows which houses those are. 

First, he sets down the determinations of the dignity of a property and its disposition. In the second part, he shows the properties found for the planet. Here he shows and says that first, in the signs, it will have some dignity or property; the first is an "accidental" property, which is when one of the planets is the Lord, Exalted, or ruler of the Triplicity, Terms, or Face. Regarding the Moon, she has these by accident. 

### The Rulership of the Signs

There are two planets that are Lords: thus **Aries** and **Scorpio** are the houses of **Mars**. **Taurus** and **Libra** are the signs where **Venus** has rulership. I am the Lord of **Gemini** <note>This refers to Mercury, though the scribe has omitted the name</note>. **Cancer** is the house of the **Moon**. **Leo** is the house of the **Sun**. **Sagittarius** and **Pisces** are the houses of **Jupiter**. **Capricorn** and **Aquarius** are the houses of **Saturn**. Furthermore, it is said that they are "proper" to their house; that is, they are the Lords there. Because the Moon and Sun are opposite to the houses of Saturn, the signs opposite to Leo and Cancer are of a contrary nature to the Sun and Moon, and the same applies to the stars.

<margin>Boundaries</margin>
Regarding others, it is said that the two signs which are the houses of any planet are in concord regarding their boundaries. 

<margin>The Circle of the Signs</margin>
The Circle of the Signs exists within the Zodiac, which is wide in the middle and bound at the poles. For imaginary works, there are parts of the imaginary signs, others you find through the primary signs and through the poles of the zodiac; the whole space is made of two joints. And just as there is one Lord, so it was exemplified in the proper binding. This concord is seen in the proper "Face" <term>Face: A subdivision of a sign (10 degrees) that gives a planet a minor dignity.</term>. First, that two signs ought to be the house of one planet; because any two signs in this way "rejoice," therefore by the authority of the explanations of the glosses with the authors, any two signs that are the houses of one planet are in concord in the zodiac according to their distance from the houses of the **Luminaries** <term>Luminaries: The Sun and the Moon, the two most important celestial bodies in medieval astrology.</term>. 

<margin>Luminaries</margin>
And in this way, it is as if they are of one planet in the region of the mind's houses. They are equally distant from Leo and Cancer, which are the houses of the Luminaries. **Taurus** and **Libra**, which are the houses of **Venus**, are equally distant from Leo, and by this, they have a concord placed between all things. 

<margin>On the concord of the signs of the brothers from the houses of the luminaries</margin>
First, he assigns that Leo is the house of the Sun and Cancer is the house of the Moon according to their proper nature. Secondly, by the two opposite signs—that is, the ones distant from the houses of the Luminaries. The Sun and Moon have two other signs that are closer or further from the heads. In the first way, the other has a good restraint on its heat so that it does not escape. They placed Leo and Cancer as the houses of the two great and noble Luminaries: Leo because it is masculine for the house of the Sun, and Cancer because it is feminine for the house of the Moon. **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer whose work was central to medieval European astrology.</note> says in his commentary, explaining those signs, that the two signs are Cancer and Gemini because they have such a moist nature, therefore he does not rejoice with Aquarius because...

The <note>zodiac</note> accords with the Sun, which heats and dries in its own way; because the Moon is feminine and nocturnal, the signs are also divided by gender and into masculine/diurnal and feminine/nocturnal. These matters speak to the Sun through the hot and dry signs, such as Leo, which is the Sun's house. Because the Moon follows the Sun, it has its own house <note>Cancer</note>, and because the Sun is named for itself, the Sun therefore has two houses <note>The text here conflates the two luminaries</note>—one for the Moon toward the East and the other for the Sun—and specifically it holds the sign of Leo, for that is one of the dry signs. Regarding the moist signs, they conversely place the house of the Moon in the moist sign of Cancer.

Furthermore, these are assigned differently: one system is taken from the order of the planets and signs, and another from their aspects <term>Aspect: The geometric angle between two planets in the sky, believed to influence their relationship.</term>. One takes precedence, and in its second proper arrangement, there are two parts of four, and these are equal houses of their own. Saturn here has two major signs distant from the houses of the two luminaries—namely, Saturn is the highest of all the planets. Capricorn and Aquarius are thus its masters because these are two signs most distant from the house of the Sun. Aquarius and Capricorn belong to Saturn, just as Capricorn <note>likely error for Scorpio</note> and Aries are the houses of Mars. They are positioned in the middle of their houses, and yet Sagittarius and Pisces are the houses of Jupiter for the same reason. Jupiter is the master of these, and so they follow in order: Aquarius, Capricorn, Sagittarius, Pisces, Scorpio, Aries, Libra, Taurus, Virgo, Gemini; then Leo and Cancer. This is the method for the houses of the luminaries and the other houses, and because the middle follows the Moon in order, and so on for the others.

Another reason by which they assign these is taken from the aspects; it is said that because Saturn is the greatest and most harmful <note>original: "deterior", meaning the "greater malefic" in astrology</note>, its house must be distant from the house of the luminaries by the opposite aspect, that is, the aspect of opposition <term>Opposition: An angle of 180 degrees, the most challenging relationship between planets.</term>. By this distance, Capricorn and Aquarius are removed from Cancer and Leo <insert>and</insert> the house of the Moon, namely Cancer, is opposite Capricorn, and Aquarius is opposite the house of the Sun, which is Leo. And Jupiter, which is better than Saturn, must have its house distant from the houses of the luminaries by a trine aspect <term>Trine: An angle of 120 degrees, considered the most harmonious and beneficial relationship.</term>, which should be one of friendship. At this distance are Sagittarius and Pisces. And Mars, which is inferior and harmful <note>the "lesser malefic"</note>, is at a square aspect <term>Square: An angle of 90 degrees, often associated with friction or conflict.</term>, and thus only from Pisces. In this way, all are assigned, and furthermore the "lesser" <note>Venus, the "lesser benefic"</note> house should be distant from the houses of the luminaries by a sextile aspect <term>Sextile: An angle of 60 degrees, viewed as a friendly or opportunistic relationship.</term>, which is an aspect of moderate quality. At this distance are Aries and Scorpio from their own, and Aries looks upon the Moon <note>unclear phrasing regarding Aries and the Moon's aspect</note>. Then Taurus and Libra likewise; and Venus is said to be better when its house is distant from the houses of the luminaries by an aspect that is one of moderate friendship. At this distance are Libra and Taurus. Libra looks upon Leo, and Taurus looks upon Cancer. And there remain Gemini and Virgo, the signs of Mercury. Because of this arrangement of the houses of the luminaries, this is also determined by elongation <term>Elongation: The angular distance of a planet from the Sun as seen from Earth.</term>—namely by the distance from the Sun according to the tables. They will be around 28 degrees. And also in these signs, as in the other four planets, they have two houses, eastern and principal. These are: Saturn rejoicing in Aquarius; Jupiter in Sagittarius; Mars in Scorpio; Venus in Taurus; Mercury in Virgo.

### And on the Exaltations of the Planets
Regarding the exaltations <term>Exaltation: A sign where a planet's influence is particularly harmonious and powerful, second only to its own house.</term> of the planets and signs: it is said that the Sun is exalted in Aries. Furthermore, they assign the exaltation of the planets in those degrees just as it is written here: Aries, 19th degree <unclear>for the Sun</unclear>. Hence it is said that if Aries is direct and the Sun is exalted within it, then the Sun’s path burns with intensity over those things standing upright, and its heat appears in the middle of that time. Libra is its "fall" <term>Fall: The sign opposite a planet's exaltation, where its influence is weakened; also called "casus."</term> at the 19th degree, because then the nights increase over the day and its heat is tempered. Similarly, because Saturn is opposite the Sun, its heat is distant by nature, and thus Libra is the exaltation of Saturn, being direct in its fall <unclear>and fall</unclear>. For the increase of the Sun in Aries is said to appear in the firmament, and that alone is the exaltation of the Moon <note>The author shifts logic to the Moon</note> and its own proper fall in the opposite sign <note>Scorpio</note>. 

Saturn governs the teeth of animals; and since it <note>Libra</note> is a rational sign, here is the exaltation of Jupiter <note>Error in text: Jupiter is exalted in Cancer</note> and the opposite sign, namely Capricorn, is its fall. And because Mars is burning by nature, when it resides in Capricorn it burns much more through Saturn <note>the ruler of Capricorn</note> toward this world; thus in Capricorn is its exaltation, and the opposite sign <note>Cancer</note> is the exaltation of Jupiter and the fall of Mars. And because Venus here imitates the heat and the greater <note>influence</note>, its exaltation is in Pisces. Its opposite is Virgo, in which is its fall. And because Mercury stays away from these and rules in Virgo, that is its exaltation; and so the opposite of the exaltation of Venus <note>Pisces</note> is its fall. Elsewhere he assigns the fall of animals differently for the same reason, but let these notes on the houses and exaltations of the planets suffice. Let this be said implicitly among those who handle the houses and exaltations of the planets, so that he may speak of ephemerides <term>Ephemeris: A table or book giving the calculated positions of celestial bodies at regular intervals.</term> and speak through aspects; that is, the astrologer dictates concerning the aspects.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of planetary dignities, moving from the houses and exaltations of the planets to the "Triplicities"—groups of three zodiac signs that share an elemental nature. It specifically details how these groupings determine planetary rulers and influence the physical world and weather.</meta>

The division of the signs is here presented in two parts: the first defines the **triplicities**, and the second defines the **aspects**.
<note>A "Triplicity" is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element: Fire, Earth, Air, or Water.</note>

It is said that the first part treats the signs and shows how every proper sign is determined by its triplicity and its totality.

### The First Triplicity
<margin>Regarding the triplicity of Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius... by day</margin>
The first part treats the triplicity in general, and the second specifically. It is said that Leo and its triplicity—meaning all those signs which are of the same nature—make one triplicity. Furthermore, Leo and Sagittarius <note>along with Aries</note> make the first triplicity because these three signs are of the same nature. 

The rulers of this triplicity <note>original: "domini triplicitatis"</note> are: 
*   **The Sun** (☉) by day. 
*   **Jupiter** (♃) by night. 
*   **Saturn** (♄) is the third, participating with the others. 

The first ruler is the Sun, the second is Jupiter, and the third is Saturn. 
<margin>by day</margin>
In the day, the 1st is the Sun, the 2nd is Jupiter, the 3rd is Saturn. In the night, the 1st is Jupiter and the others follow. 

The first sign <note>Aries</note> produces a temperate heat; the second, Leo, produces a glowing heat; the third, Sagittarius, produces a parching heat. 
<margin>at night</margin>
When one of these signs is in the **Ascendant** <term>Ascendant: The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment</term> or in **Opposition** <term>Opposition: An aspect where two planets or points are 180 degrees apart</term> to the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note> during the winter, it signifies a warm spell; in the summer, it signifies excessive heat, especially if the rulers of that sign are present in that sign or in an angle.

### The Second Triplicity
<margin>The 2nd Triplicity: Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn</margin>
Next is the second triplicity. **Virgo and Capricorn** <note>along with Taurus</note> make the second triplicity, which are all of the same nature. These are feminine, nocturnal signs: cold and dry, melancholic, and of an acid taste. 

The rulers of this triplicity are:
*   **Venus** (♀) by day.
*   **The Moon** (☽) by night.
*   **Mars** (♂) is the third participating ruler.

According to **Albumasar** <note>original: "Albumasar," the famous Persian astrologer (787–886 AD)</note>, this triplicity produces a temperate coldness that strengthens other things. The second sign produces a glowing cold, and the third a parching or biting cold. When any of these fall in the Ascendant or in Opposition to the luminaries in winter, there will be great cold, especially if Saturn is the ruler of the time.

### The Third Triplicity
<margin>The 3rd Triplicity: Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius</margin>
The third triplicity consists of **Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius**, which are of a masculine, diurnal, and sanguine nature. They are hot and moist, airy, western, and of a sweet taste.

The rulers are:
*   **Saturn** (♄) by day.
*   **Mercury** (☿) by night.
*   **Jupiter** (♃) is the third participant.

According to Albumasar, the first sign of this triplicity produces temperate and strengthening sweet winds; the second produces sharp winds; the third produces dissipating winds. When any of these signs are ascending in the hour when the Moon is in opposition, you may understand the effects by that opposition.

### The Fourth Triplicity
<margin>The 4th Triplicity: Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces</margin>
Next is the fourth triplicity, consisting of **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces**. These are all feminine, nocturnal, phlegmatic, and watery signs: cold and moist with a salty taste.

The rulers are:
*   **Venus** (♀) by day.
*   **Mars** (♂) by night.
*   **The Moon** (☽) is the third participant.

According to Albumasar, the first produces temperate rain; the second, nocturnal moisture; the third is destructive. When any of these are in the Ascendant or in Opposition to the luminaries, it indicates moisture and rain. 
<margin>Concerning rain</margin>
If the water signs are in the Ascendant, or in the angles of the chart at the time of the lunar conjunction or opposition, there will be much rain in that year. But if the lunar positions are in "fall" <note>weak positions</note> and not in the angles, rain will not descend much in that month or for the greater part of the year. 

I have experienced this regarding rain: when a watery sign is in the Ascendant at the time of the opposition, and the Moon is in that same sign, it is a time of rain that lasts as long as the Moon stays in that sign. This is according to the empirical teachings of **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abrahām Aueneze," the 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer</note> and Albumasar, which bring much joy when their truth is tested. Albumasar says that if the ascending sign is in the angles, it indicates the diversity of the regions. If they are not in the angles, there will be mists without rain.

Having finished the triplicities, we shall next discuss the aspects. Therefore, we pass on.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how zodiac signs are grouped. Having previously covered the elements and triplicities, the text now introduces the "modalities" (moveable, fixed, and common) and the "aspects" (the geometric angles between planets).</meta>

<margin>
Signs which are moveable, fixed, or common
</margin>

From here, it is said that four signs are categorized according to their mode: some are **fixed**, some are **middle** (also called **common** <gloss>1</gloss>), and others are **moveable**. It is noted that this arrangement is found in the teachings of Ptolemy <note>original: "ptholo"; refers to Claudius Ptolemy, the foundational authority for medieval astrology</note> in his second book. He proposes that these modes determine how things begin, continue, or change. For instance, the **fixed signs** are necessary for stability, such as when one intends to build houses; the **moveable signs** indicate change and movement. Therefore, all these signs previously mentioned are categorized here most clearly... because a victory is signified when the lords of the signs are free from "evil" planetary houses...

<margin>
Triplicities and planets in the signs; Aspects
</margin>

Regarding the time of the **aspects** <term>Aspect: The specific geometric angle between two planets that determines how they influence each other</term>, this section determines how they are defined. First, it treats the aspects themselves; second, it treats the "projections of rays" <note>the way planets are thought to 'beam' their influence to other parts of the zodiac</note>. 

The text determines:
1.  The **Conjunction** <note>represented by the symbol $\sigma$ in the text, though contextually discussing the meeting of rays</note>.
2.  The **Square** <note>symbol $\square$; also called "quadrature"</note>.
3.  The **Trine** <note>symbol $\triangle$; a 120-degree angle</note>.
4.  The **Sextile** <note>symbol $\ast$; a 60-degree angle</note>.

It explains that every sign "beholds" or aspects the others in a specific way. For example, a sign aspects the third sign from itself <note>inclusive counting</note> in a certain manner, and the sign at a distance of one-third of the circle <note>the Trine</note> is described as having a specific temperament or "participation."

<margin>
Why two signs in an aspect agree in one quality
</margin>

Two signs might seem to be in discord, yet they agree in one quality. This is for the following reason: they may share a "masculine" nature or "heat." For example, **Aries** (♈︎) and **Leo** (♌︎) both agree in being hot and masculine. **Taurus** (♉︎) and **Pisces** (♓︎) both agree in being cold and feminine. This should be understood for all signs and the planets that inhabit them. These relationships are called "tetragons" <note>referring to the four-sided relationship of the square aspect</note> when they share these specific distances.

<margin>
Concerning the Square aspect ($\square$)
</margin>

Thirdly, regarding the **Square** aspect <note>original: "quadratura"</note>: signs at this distance are said to be "repugnant" to one another. This is because they differ in their primary qualities. This is especially important in the study of acute diseases; one must look at the sign where the aspect falls. If there is a great repugnance in their qualities, it signifies a struggle for health. If the aspect falls in **Sagittarius** (♐︎), which is a human sign <note>symbolized by the archer/centaur</note>, there may not be as much repugnance as there is with **Taurus** (♉︎), which is a "brutish" sign. These differences in heat, cold, and gender determine whether the outcome leads to recovery or death, according to the "fortunes" or "misfortunes" <note>benefic or malefic planets</note> involved.

<margin>
Concerning the Trine aspect ($\triangle$)
</margin>

Fourthly, we speak of the **Trine** aspect. This occurs when signs are at a distance of 120 degrees from one another. This aspect is considered "amicable" because signs at this distance belong to the same **triplicity** and thus share the same nature.

<margin>
The Sextile aspect ($\ast$)
</margin>

Regarding the **Sextile** aspect: it is similar in nature but occurs at a distance of 60 degrees. It is less powerful than the Trine but still represents a form of agreement.

<margin>
Opposition and Conjunction ($\sigma$)
</margin>

Opposition occurs at 180 degrees. Ptolemy teaches that an aspect is considered active when planets are within 10 degrees of the exact point. If a planet is "leading" and the other "follows," the aspect remains strong. These aspects vary in duration; for instance, those occurring in **Taurus** (♉︎) have a different "ascension" or duration than others.

<margin>
The Projection of Rays
</margin>

At 60 degrees, a planet "aspects" by projecting its rays. This part of the text explains the "projections of rays," meaning how a planet in one sign sends its power to a specific degree in another sign. 

<margin>
The consideration of the aspect, which is threefold
</margin>

The consideration of the aspect is done in three ways. This speaks to the strength and the manner in which the planets communicate their significance through these rays.

<margin>
Planetary dignities <note>original: "Dignitates planetarum"</note>
</margin>

### Concerning the Dignities of the Planets
Regarding the dignities of the planets, it appears that a planet resides in its own house, or sometimes is exalted in its own house and in its <term explanation="A planet's point of greatest strength and influence in the zodiac">exaltation</term>. And many reside in their kingdoms and their <term explanation="A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element—fire, earth, air, or water—each ruled by specific planets">triplicities</term>. From this, it should be noted that a planet suffers greater misfortune when it is in the house or exaltation of a "detestable member" <note>likely referring to a planet in its "fall" or "detriment," where its influence is weakened</note> unless it is strong in its own kingdom and in a place of strength. Therefore, when a planet is found in its own houses and exaltations, it is a sign of good fortune; otherwise, it is a sign of evil. They have taught by this figure that there are two differences concerning the dignities of planets in the signs and the strength they possess within those dignities.

In this section, we treat the figures or forms of the signs themselves, which show us which signs have a human form and which have the forms of other animals. Some are called "human" according to the images they represent. These are Gemini, Aquarius, Libra, and the first half of Sagittarius. These are called human because of their power and because they are common to humanity. They are often associated with the East. 

Certain signs are called "animal-like" or "domestic," and these are the ones depicted in the figures of domestic animals, such as Aries (the Ram), Taurus (the Bull), and Capricorn (the Goat). Some are said to have a "great aspect" <note>original: "magf aspz," likely "magnus aspectus"</note> when they appear in the providential part toward the back of the Bull. 

Other signs are called "crooked" or "twisted," such as Aries, Taurus, Scorpio, Sagittarius, and Capricorn. There are also signs called "signs of many children" <note>original: "multoz filioz," meaning fertile or fruitful signs</note>, which are Scorpio and Pisces. Some are "sterile," namely Leo and Virgo. Others are called signs of "few children," such as Aries, Taurus, Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aquarius. Some signs are considered very "lecherous," such as Aries, Taurus, Leo, and Capricorn. Certain signs are said to have the "diameter of a wheel," having long animal forms, such as Aries, Taurus, Leo, Capricorn, and part of Sagittarius. Finally, some signs are called "cardinal," which are those figured according to images of rare things, such as Scorpio and Pisces.

Haly Abenragel <note>An influential Arab astrologer whose work 'De Iudiciis Astrorum' was a standard textbook in medieval Europe</note> briefly explained the forms of the signs: some have human form, some the form of beasts, and others the form of reptiles. The human-like signs are Gemini, Aquarius, and Virgo. Those with the form of beasts are Taurus, Capricorn, and Sagittarius (specifically the horse-like part) and the lion-like Leo. Those with the form of reptiles are Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces.

<margin>
The division of the earth by lines according to the way of the world <note>original: "Divisio ter̄ p̄ leneas s̄m̄ modū mūti"</note>
</margin>
<margin>
Description of the lines
</margin>

Since we have finished with the figures of the signs and what they show regarding human illness and health, we now divide the discussion into two parts. First, we speak of the colors of the planets and signs; second, we speak of the parts of the earth they signify. The world is divided into 12 parts according to the 12 signs. 

It is clear that <gloss>names</gloss> of the earth are noted here. The entire habitable earth is situated in four parts, and this follows a "proper division." Imagine a line that passes from the East to the West through the middle of the habitation, so that this line divides the southern part from the northern part. This line is said to be at a distance of 36 degrees from the equator. According to this division, it is 30 degrees from the farthest point of habitation in the North. Thus, the total latitude is 66 degrees. This distance is the same as the distance from the equator to the Arctic Circle, which is 66 degrees and 36 minutes (or 30 minutes in some calculations). 

According to Haly, this line provides a passage for mankind. Where the line passes through the "Hyperborean" <note>The far north</note> regions, it makes a greater effect so that men on one shore toward the south look toward those on the other. It is said there is an island where one part is hidden in the Hyperborean mists, and the Holy Land stands within it, held as if in a hand. This is shown to demonstrate that beyond that place, there is no habitation on any islands. The same holds true in the Eastern part; at the end of the aforementioned line, it is demonstrated that there is no habitation beyond that place. 

You should understand that men placed these landmarks in figures so that the whole world might be described. Let us read of the aforementioned line: it passes through the meridian where this line is imagined through the middle of the earth, emanating 90 degrees from the East and another 90 degrees from the opposite side. Then imagine another line through the poles of the world, crossing the first line so that it passes through the middle of the habitable earth according to its length. It is clear, therefore, that these two lines we have described...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of astrological influences on the world, moving from the specific qualities of signs to their geographical associations and their influence on human physiology. It introduces the "triplicities" (groups of three signs) and their governance over specific regions and "climates" (latitudinal zones), eventually citing the influential medieval scholar Abraham ibn Ezra (Avenzra).</meta>

Let the entire habitable earth be divided into 12 parts, which parts correspond to the lower area of the lines that are designated within the habitable earth. This division having been understood, it is easy to see the form of the <term explanation="A grouping of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element—Fire, Earth, Air, or Water—each of which is roughly 120 degrees apart">triplicities</term> in the particular signs mentioned before. Just as the triplicities which have these signs—Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius—form one triplicity. This group pertains to the Eastern part of the habitable world which is said to be between... <insert>he who</insert> governs it is Jupiter, because that same sign also has Mars as a ruler over them. This body pertains to the Eastern part.

Secondly, the signs of the [next] triplicity—namely Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn—pertain to the part that is between the South and the East. Venus governs this, because it is common to the South and has leadership in that direction, just as it pertains to the Eastern part. And the third triplicity—namely Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius—pertains to the part which is called between the East and the North. Saturn governs this; the body pertains to the East and has leadership in it, while Jupiter pertains to the North. And the fourth sign, which is the triplicity of Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces, pertains to the part which is between the West and the South. Mars governs this because it pertains to the West, and Venus has leadership in it. From the aforementioned, one can prognosticate to which people a land pertains. Just as the Latins and Greeks speak of certain things, such as Egypt: all its land and latitude is at 30 degrees, and its latitude finishes at 19 degrees from the equator... and one must think of others in their own way. For a land is said to be diverse according to the work of the lord who holds the sign of that triplicity which is over that region. One can know from these three factors what is experienced through the behavior and customs of the men inhabiting it. Also, if one wishes to know how a land is experienced, it varies in its rational part.

<margin>
Which signs dominate over the major parts of the earth
</margin>

I perceive that Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius dominate over it [this region]. And if you wish to know over which part any of these signs dominates, look to the behavior and customs of the men according to the direction of the lands which the sign most accords with. For example, it is shown through Rome and its fame and the nobility of that part, that the most noble signs are attributed to them. Thus Leo has the <term explanation="The zodiac sign where a planet is most 'at home' and powerful">house</term> of the Sun. Because of this, the Germans <note>original: "almani"</note> are also furious in their pursuit of honor, following the nature of Mars; therefore, Aries is attributed to them according to Mars. It is also evident that the Spaniards are good soldiers and great fighters in arms, therefore Sagittarius is attributed to them because it is a mixture of the fury of wars. It has the protection... in that second quadruped part. And first, Aries accords with it and the land of Britain, and the land of the Palatinate, and that which ought to be said of France <note>original: "f'rama," likely 'Francia'</note> and of my own land. Leo accords with Italy, Gaul, Apulia, and Sicily <note>Note: Apulia and Sicily were major southern Italian kingdoms</note>; and others say that all these belong to Rome. And that which accords with Sagittarius is the land of Crete and Spain. Regarding the protection of all signs in other lands, I provide notice that if we understand the capture and direction according to men, as in the movement it makes in the soul, whether toward manliness or severity, all [this] is recognized in them; and those who wish to dwell in them should adapt themselves according to the manner of the rulers in those aforementioned signs.

<margin>
Which parts each of the five climates possess
</margin>

According to the opinion of Abraham Avenzra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar, poet, and astrologer whose work heavily influenced Latin science</note>, the first <term explanation="An ancient geographical system dividing the world into seven horizontal bands or 'climates' based on the length of the longest day">climate</term> belongs to Capricorn and Aquarius, and its governors are Saturn and Mars; and Sagittarius and Pisces, and its governor is Jupiter. The second climate is more specific by the direction of its governors under Mars. The fourth climate belongs to Leo and is governed by the Sun. The fifth climate belongs to Taurus and Libra and its governor is Venus. The sixth climate belongs to Gemini and Virgo, and its governor is Mercury. The seventh climate belongs to Cancer and its governor is the Moon.

Abraham Avenzra also places the degrees of those being born under any sign, according to their physical form. He says: if one was born under the first <term explanation="A 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign, also known as a 'decan'">face</term> of Aries, he is reddish and pale, his belly and fists are lean in flesh, and he will have a mark upon his foot or his left hand. This is according to the triplicity and the time directed by Mars. For those who are born under its second face, the body was perfected in the manner of the first face, but they have a bad will in their eyes, and other things that need correcting. If he was born under its third face, he is of a reddish color and [his skin] is folded or wrinkled.

If one was born under the first face of Taurus, he will be of short stature, his eyes large, his lips thick, and he will have a mark on his neck... If born under the second face, he will have a round face, and the second face makes the side of the eyes beautiful, and his soul is very willful, so that he proceeds quickly...

<margin>1st face</margin>
When someone originates from the first face <note>original: "facie," referring to the decan, a ten-degree division of a zodiac sign</note> of **Pisces**, they take after the fish: the entire body is either white <note>pale-skinned</note> or the face is similarly white and broad. In this first face, the part of the face should be washed; his eyes are more black than white, and he will have a better face but will eventually grow weak. 
<margin>2nd face</margin>
The second face is sleepy and gluttonous; such a person has a mark on their nose <note>original: "rostro," literally "beak" or "snout," used here for the human nose</note> from the time of their birth. On the face and the "arm" of the forehead <note>likely the temple or brow ridge</note> they have a handsome look; they have a hairy beard and will be a wanderer in the dunes. This is a son of man born under the Lord **Jupiter** (♃). 
<margin>3rd face</margin>
In the third face, the person present has a clear appearance; their teeth are beautiful, and they are not sickly.

He divides twelve parts for the twelve signs. Where these parts rule is evident: the first and two [others] according to proportion, and particularly where they are led and have dominion. 

<margin>Concerning infirmities: how one shall recognize a person from the dispositions of the planets and signs</margin>

By these signs, one may know which infirmity someone is liable for in the human body. Finally, concerning the members, it is clearly shown how they suffer. According to that debility and torment—and if fate decrees it for many—that infirmity is inspected through the faces of the signs. By the "weight," understand those members in a person's nature which I speak of as natural. 

Regarding the births of those with [weak] lungs, it is a sign [of the stars]; many are led with the "lung" in the head, and if it is so, many [have it] in the neck. Understand the other signs in proportion. All many members in which diseases fall and obstacles or damage are retained [can be seen] from the figure, whether in a man born [then] or according to the bile <term>choln: likely a reference to the "choleric" humor or yellow bile</term> under which they were born. The author speaks diffusely on this matter.

14 [degrees] which are called "parents" <note>perhaps "leading" degrees</note> at first increase fortune. And **Ptolemy** <note>The 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian polymath whose "Tetrabiblos" was the foundation of Western astrology</note> teaches us that doctrine concerning the origin, by which means detriment comes from evil or good, and the alterations according to the order of the qualities. Medical astrology <note>original: "medic' p' ap' log'" - likely *medicina per astrologiam*</note> and the movement of the stars seek to understand the nature and causes of **acute diseases**, occurring on the 7th day, the 14th day, or the 21st day. At first, it is said that through hearing and doctrine, without which nothing is transformed, one learns from the experience of the end.

**Ptolemy** demonstrates that a disease is changed according to the cause. It is repugnant to honor the hour <unclear>o'apa'</unclear> if it is expected in an opportune place, specifically the place the Moon was in at the beginning of the disease. At that time, it is no more honorable because it moves as it did at the start of the illness. It does not change but resists the patient with an accusation of weakness, and in a place where one lacks helpers. One expects that the Moon is in the sign in which it was captured, or in opposition to that sign. This is according to the nature of the Moon's movement through the signs, which signifies enmity and the length of the disease.

Here, the physicians of the stars <note>astrological physicians</note> determine the figures of the illness. The **first day** is the 7th, when the Moon is in a square aspect <note>original: "u'ico" - likely referring to the 90-degree square aspect</note> to its position at the start of the illness. This is an inopportune time. The second critical time of the disease is the 14th day <note>when the Moon is in opposition, 180 degrees from the start</note>, and the third is the 21st day <note>the second square</note>.

This method of other physicians follows the points of the angles. One line is different from the other; one point is indicative. When the Moon reaches the point that marks the progression, it shows the latitude in which the person's health sits. If it is in the eight angles, these points are contrary or favorable for the disease according to nature. Observe the fixed stars <term>fixed stars</term><note>Stars that appear not to move relative to each other, unlike "wandering stars" or planets</note> that are in conjunction; if they are of a strong nature, they may induce death. But if they stand for victory over **cholera** <note>In medieval medicine, "cholera" or yellow bile was one of the four humors; an excess caused hot, dry diseases</note>, then nature will overcome the cholera. If the stars are contrary to the disease, the person will remain strong in their nature, for that which is contrary to the disease ends it—such as a cold influence for a hot disease.

The Moon is the most important factor in **acute diseases**, more than the Sun <note>original: "orbis solis"</note>. All this was useful to us from the sayings of **Ptolemy** concerning all the stars and diseases. This is the doctrine given to us: if a disease follows its usual course, it is not a defect of the order of the stars. This is explained in the book of **Ptolemy** and **Hippocrates** <note>original: "ypoc't'" - the Greek "Father of Medicine" whose Aphorisms were central to medieval medical training</note>. Nature reports to us in the books of Ptolemy and **Haly [Abenragel]** <note>A 11th-century Arab astrologer whose "De Iudiciis Astrorum" was a standard textbook</note> concerning the 7th, 14th, and 21st days. These are the **critical days** <term>critical days</term><note>original: "dies cidia" - *dies critica*. Specific days when a disease was expected to turn toward recovery or death</note> because the Moon on the 14th day reaches the opposite aspect of the place it occupied at the beginning of the illness. On the 21st day, it reaches the second square aspect.

**Haly** says: when the astrologer wishes to judge the critical day, he must observe the time when the Moon arrives at the square aspect of the place it was in at the beginning of the disease. If it is joined with a favorable planet <note>original: "espe u' laudab'le"</note> or with fixed stars that are of a good nature, it signifies a good outcome. But if it is joined with an unfortunate influence, it signifies the middle of the disease, or even its end in the subject's death.
